title: Susi and Chuma Carry Livingstone Home
text:
On 1 May 1873, in the village of Chitambo in what is now Zambia, the Scottish missionary and explorer David Livingstone was found dead, kneeling by his bed. He had been searching for the source of the Nile and was worn out by years of illness.

His African companions, led by Abdullah Susi and James Chuma, who had traveled with him for years, decided that his body must be taken home. It was a dangerous choice. The journey to the coast was over a thousand miles through territory where carrying a corpse could provoke fear and hostility. They buried his heart under a tree at Chitambo, preserved the body with salt and by drying it in the sun, wrapped it, and enclosed it in a cylinder of bark covered with sailcloth.

For months the party, some sixty people, carried Livingstone's body, his journals and his instruments toward the Indian Ocean. On the way they met a British relief expedition whose leader urged them to bury the body in the interior. They refused and went on.

In February 1874 they reached Bagamoyo on the coast, and the body was shipped to England. Livingstone was buried in Westminster Abbey in April 1874. Susi and Chuma were later brought to England, where they helped Horace Waller prepare Livingstone's last journals for publication, and their account of the journey was printed with them.
lesson: A team's loyalty can carry a mission past its leader's death. Those who seem like followers are often the ones who finish the work.
people: Abdullah Susi, James Chuma, Jacob Wainwright, David Livingstone
source: Horace Waller, ed., The Last Journals of David Livingstone (1874)
